extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century London literate public interested in manners, theatre, and morals
extracted.subtask_description: Short journalistic essays offering social commentary and criticism of public entertainments, household manners, and private conduct in early-18th-century London. The pieces evaluate acting, stagecraft, masquerade behaviour, audience taste, and domestic civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discreet household service and lodging etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: A householder/landlady should accommodate a lodger's humour and routines quietly — e.g. 'my Coffee comes into my Chamber every Morning without asking' and responding to nonverbal signals ('if I want Fire I point to my Chimney').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive example: the Widow-woman who supplies coffee, fire, water, and restrains ceremonious salutations so the lodger moves 'with the same Liberty as a Cat'. Anti-pattern: an 'officious Land-lady' who repeatedly asks intrusive questions (e.g. how one has slept) and forces a lodger to change rooms. Implication: good household management prioritizes discretion, unobtrusive service, and preservation of a lodger's privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize ceremonious attention to preserve guest comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive ceremony (rising when a guest comes in, interruptive greetings) which can embarrass or inconvenience visitors: the author notes his landlady forbade servants from rising because he 'always cried Pish and went out again.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: tailor household customs to guests' temperaments; remove needless formalities that make guests uncomfortable. Example anti-pattern: servants all rising to the guest every time he enters, causing him to leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect children from terrifying tales (preserve sound imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should be guarded against 'little Horrours of Imagination' (ghost stories etc.) that can produce lasting fear; a sound imagination is a great blessing next to clear judgment and conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of harm: soldiers frightened by their own shadows, persons 'terrify'd, even to Distraction' by harmless sights. Remedy: 'arm our selves against them by the Dictates of Reason and Religion' and 'pull the old Woman out of our Hearts' (i.e., extinguish superstitious notions). Practical rule: avoid exposing the young to ghost stories and cultivate rational/religious reassurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting: expressive use of body and face
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors should 'make the same use of their Arms and Legs, and inform their Faces with as significant Looks and Passions' — physical action gives dignity and can redeem forced or cold lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive model: Signior Nicolini's action, which 'gives new Majesty to Kings, Resolution to Heroes, and Softness to Lovers.' Guidance to English tragedians: adopt expressive physicality to lend weight to dialogue and elevate the drama. Anti-pattern: stiff performers whose faces or limbs fail to convey passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal suitability for roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocal quality must fit the character: the author complains that 'by the Squeak of their Voices the Heroes of each are Eunuchs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select performers with voices appropriate to heroic or masculine parts; avoid casting where voice undermines character credibility. Example: thin or squeaking voices on heroic roles are conspicuous flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft coherence: scenery, cues, and props must be managed
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery and mechanical effects should be coherent and timely (thunder/lightning, side-scene changes), and stage illusions should not produce incongruities (e.g. a man in a full-bottomed wig appearing 'in the Midst of the Sea').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive examples: the boy directing painted dragons who 'made them spit Fire and Smoke' with 'just Proportions' and timing. Anti-patterns: forgetting to change side-scenes, clumsy thunder/lightning, mismatched scenic elements that break audience immersion. Practical rule: coordinate scene changes and stage machinery carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal actors must be disciplined and reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: If animals are employed on stage, they must be trained to perform their parts (contrast: 'Sparrows and Chaffinches... fly as yet very irregularly' vs. Powell's pig that 'danc[es] a Minuet together').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: only introduce animals when they can be reliably managed; undisciplined animals distract, put out candles, or ruin scenes. Reward for good training: animals that enhance spectacle without disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage audience expectations; avoid overpromising in bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed programmes or bills that raise excessive expectations risk disappointing audiences — 'the Undertakers... having raised too great an Expectation in their printed Opera, very much disappointed their Audience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: either omit a detailed bill of fare so each scene feels new (positive example: Mr Powell's avoidance of a beforehand bill), or ensure that advertised spectacles can actually be delivered to avoid audience resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for performance in the audience's native language
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances in the native tongue are preferable for engagement and understanding: 'I must prefer the Performance of Mr Powell, because it is in our own Language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming in the vernacular improves accessibility and audience enjoyment; foreign-language entertainments may dazzle but risk losing the public's comprehension and sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masquerade/role-play etiquette: preserve character consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Attendees at masquerades should 'be able to say or do things proper for the Dress in which he appears'; dressing as a character obliges one to act that part, or else the spectacle degrades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of poor practice: Roman Senators who behave like rakes, philosophers rendered speechless, judges dancing minuets with Quaker partners. Rule: maintain character coherence in costume, speech, and behaviour to raise the elegance and instructive quality of masquerades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse or indecorous humour that violates a piece's moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic or satirical elements should not subvert the intended moral or become offensively coarse (e.g. 'Punch's national Reflections on the French' or King Harry's 'laying his Leg upon his Queen's Lap' are cited as violations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess entertainment for whether humor undermines moral aims or public decency. Anti-pattern: crude national reflections, indecorous bodily antics that offend or break the moral tone of a piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept theatrical conventions and backstage collegiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatre operates by conventions (dropped actors 'dead' onstage who later 'sit peaceably by one another' behind the scenes); such practices need not be treated as deceitful — they are part of dramatic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging theatrical events, distinguish onstage representation from offstage reality. Criticism that confuses theatrical convention with personal hypocrisy is misplaced; example: Nicolini and the lion smoking together after a staged combat is not proof the combat is a sham in an injurious sense, but a normal backstage collegiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value inner virtues and private felicity over external show
rubrics_metrics.description: True happiness comes from private companionship, good sense, and orderly domestic life rather than pomp, equipage, or showy appearances ('True Happiness is of a retired Nature... It loves Shade and Solitude').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social standard: judge persons by their private virtues (friendship, regular household economy, good sense) rather than by external trappings (coaches, lace, jewelry). Anti-pattern: being 'smitten with every thing that is showy and superficial' — leads to folly and domestic ruin.
